extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (Math 216) and others learning foundations of algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, definitions, and tests for geometric properties of schemes and morphisms (geometric points/fibers, geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced, radicial maps, normalization, and finiteness of integral closure). Primarily aimed at verifying these properties via base change and reduction-to-finite-type tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric point
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric point of a scheme X is defined to be a morphism Spec k -> X where k is an algebraically closed field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric points are a flavor of scheme-valued points and are an enriched version of a plain point (a point together with an inclusion of its residue field into an algebraically closed field). Warning: some sources use 'separably closed' instead of 'algebraically closed' in this definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric fiber and geometrically X-properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A geometric fiber of a morphism X -> Y is the fiber over a geometric point of Y. A morphism has connected (resp. irreducible, integral, reduced) geometric fibers if all its geometric fibers are connected (resp. irreducible, integral, reduced). One usually says the morphism has geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced fibers. A k-scheme X is geometrically connected/irreducible/integral/reduced if the structure morphism X -> Spec k has those geometrically-qualitied fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the principal geometric properties studied here; many results show how to check/preserve them under base change and field extensions. Examples given include Spec C over Spec R (geometrically reduced but not geometrically irreducible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent tests for geometric reducedness (Ra–Rd)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the following statements about a k-scheme X (for 'X_K' denoting base change to field K): (Ra) X_K is reduced for all fields K. (Rb) X_K is reduced for all algebraically closed fields K (i.e., X is geometrically reduced). (Rc) X_k is reduced for K = k. (Rd) X_{k^p} is reduced (where k^p is the perfect closure of k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivially (Ra) => (Rb) => (Rc) and (Ra) => (Rd). The text states the 'hard fact' that (Rd) => (Ra), hence all four are equivalent; the exercises and propositions give the steps to prove these implications. Use the tensor-finiteness trick to reduce to finite-type situations when proving implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent tests for geometric irreducibility (Ia–Id)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous to the reduced case: (Ia) X_K is irreducible for all fields K. (Ib) X_K is irreducible for all algebraically closed fields K (i.e., X is geometrically irreducible). (Ic) X_k is irreducible for K = k. (Id) X_{k^s} is irreducible (where k^s is the separable closure of k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial implications mirror the reduced case; the text proves the nontrivial implication (Id) => (Ia) (and hence equivalence) using reduction to finite type, separable/normal closures, and the tensor-finiteness trick. Exercises guide checking these implications in detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent tests for geometric connectedness (Ca–Cd)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarly: (Ca) X_K is connected for all fields K. (Cb) X_K is connected for all algebraically closed fields K (i.e., X is geometrically connected). (Cc) X_k is connected for K = k. (Cd) X_{k^s} is connected (k^s separable closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again, trivial implications hold and the hard fact is that (Cd) => (Ca), making the four statements equivalent. Lemmas and propositions (e.g., 9.5.9–9.5.11) show how connectedness can be checked after base change, especially over separably closed fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensor-finiteness trick (reduction to finitely generated subrings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving properties that are preserved under base change, one can replace rings by finitely generated subrings generated by a finite number of elements appearing in a computation (e.g., a representative of an idempotent or element written as a sum of decomposable tensors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trick is used repeatedly to reduce general statements to the finite-type case, where propositions like openness of maps and finiteness arguments are available. Example uses: proving openness of maps, reducing idempotent checks to finite-type rings, and treating base-change arguments using Spec of finitely generated algebras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely inseparable extensions give homeomorphisms on base-change (Lemma 9.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the field extension E/F is purely inseparable and X is any F-scheme, then the natural map φ: X_E -> X is a homeomorphism (on underlying topological spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: φ is bijective (points correspond), scheme-theoretic fibers are single points, φ is continuous, and by Lemma 9.5.6 φ is open. This fact is used to relate geometric properties under purely inseparable extensions and to motivate using separable/perfect closures in equivalence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of connectedness and irreducibility over separably-closed fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 9.5.10 / Corollary 9.5.11: If k is separably closed and Spec A (or Y) is connected, then Spec A (or Y) is geometrically connected over k. Proposition 9.5.13 / 9.5.14: If k is separably closed and A has Spec A irreducible, then base-change to any field extension K/k gives Spec(A ⊗_k K) irreducible; hence irreducibility is preserved for separably-closed base fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use the tensor-finiteness trick and the fact that base-change maps are open; reduce to finite-type cases and use images in the base to find contradictions if disconnected/ reducible. These give practical checks: over separably-closed k, checking connectedness/irreducibility is easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of reducedness under base-change (perfect/separable hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions 9.5.17–9.5.20 and Corollary 9.5.21: (a) If B is geometrically reduced and A is reduced, then A ⊗_k B is reduced. (b) For A reduced, A ⊗_k k(t) is reduced; if E/k finite separable, then A ⊗_k E is reduced. (c) If E/k is an extension of a perfect field and X is a reduced k-scheme, then X_E is reduced. (d) If k is perfect and A,B are reduced k-algebras then A ⊗_k B is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: reduce to the affine case and to A a product of fields (function fields of components), then apply definitions. Use Algebraic Fact 9.5.16 about finitely generated extensions of perfect fields factoring into finite separable and purely transcendental parts. These results provide tests and constructions ensuring reducedness after base-change under the stated hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universally injective (radicial) morphisms: definition and equivalent criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is universally injective if it is injective on underlying sets after any base change (traditionally called 'radicial'). For a morphism π: X -> Y the following are equivalent: (i) π is universally injective; (ii) for every field K the induced map Hom(Spec K, X) -> Hom(Spec K, Y) is injective (so universally injective = injective on geometric points); (iii) for each p ∈ X, the field extension κ(p)/κ(π(p)) is purely inseparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universally injective morphisms generalize purely inseparable field extensions; examples include locally closed embeddings and more generally monomorphisms. The class is stable under composition, base change, products, and is local on the target. Exercises show how to connect the three equivalent formulations and observe that it suffices to check K algebraically closed in (ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization: definition, universal property, uniqueness and existence (affine case)
rubrics_metrics.description: A normalization of a reduced scheme X is a morphism ν: X^ν -> X from a normal scheme X^ν that induces a bijection of irreducible components and is birational on each irreducible component; it satisfies a universal property and is unique up to unique isomorphism. For X = Spec A (A integral), the normalization is Spec of the integral closure of A in its fraction field K(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction for affine X: take integral closure of A in its fraction field (elements integral over A). Exercises show the universal property and that global sections of irreducible normal schemes are integrally closed. Existence in general integral schemes is given (exercise 9.7.B) by gluing affine normalizations; details use fiber product ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of normalization (integrality, surjectivity, birationality, finiteness on finite-type schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalization morphisms are integral and surjective. If X is an integral finite-type k-scheme, its normalization ν: X^ν -> X is birational and (in finite separable extension cases) finite. For integral finite-type k-schemes, the normalization is an isomorphism on an open dense subset of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises show: (a) normalizations of integral schemes exist; (b) normalizations are integral and surjective (use Lying Over); (c) normalization is birational for finite-type integral k-schemes; (d) normalization is finite when normalizing in a finite separable field extension or when A is a finitely generated k-algebra (use Theorem 9.7.3). Geometric examples (node, cusp, tacnode) illustrate how normalization 'resolves' curve singularities in dimension 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of integral closure (Theorem 9.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is a Noetherian integral domain, K = K(A), L/K is a finite field extension, and B is the integral closure of A in L. (a) If A is integrally closed and L/K is separable, then B is a finitely generated A-module. (b) If A is a finitely generated k-algebra, then B is a finitely generated A-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch proofs use reduction to Galois extensions (part (a)) and Noether Normalization (part (b)) together with the tensor-finiteness trick. The theorem is central to showing that normalizations of varieties (finite-type schemes over fields) are finite morphisms and hence are varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: integral closure of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian
rubrics_metrics.description: Part (b) of the finiteness theorem does not hold for arbitrary Noetherian A: the integral closure of a Noetherian ring need not be Noetherian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a caution when applying finiteness results: additional hypotheses (e.g., A finitely generated over a field, or separability hypotheses) are necessary to guarantee that integral closure is finite/Noetherian. Examples and references are given in the text.
